(CNN) -- The Marine accused of killing Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach, who was more than eight months pregnant, was not the father of her unborn child, a law enforcement source close to the murder investigation said Saturday. Marine Cpl. Cesar Laurean, who is being held on a murder charge, is scheduled for arraignment in June. The source, who has seen a report completed earlier this month by the Defense Department's Armed Forces Institute of Pathology, said Cpl. Cesar Laurean's DNA does not match that of the unborn child, who also died. Laurean and Lauterbach were stationed at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. An autopsy showed that Lauterbach, 20, died of blunt force trauma to the head. Police unearthed her charred body from beneath a barbecue pit in Laurean's backyard in January 2008. She disappeared the month before. Laurean was 22 when he was arrested in Mexico in April 2008. At the time, a Mexican reporter asked Laurean whether he had killed Lauterbach. The Marine replied, "I loved her." Laurean has been indicted on charges that include first-degree murder, financial card transaction fraud and obtaining property by false pretenses. North Carolina prosecutors allege he killed Lauterbach on December 14 and used her ATM card 10 days later before fleeing to Mexico. He holds dual citizenship in the United States and Mexico. The law enforcement source familiar with the case said a DNA swab was taken by court order from Laurean after he was extradited from Mexico in March to face charges in North Carolina. Mexican authorities agreed to the extradition, in part because prosecutors took the death penalty off the table. Mexico does not have a death penalty. Before her death, Lauterbach told the Marines that Laurean raped her. The month before she disappeared, Lauterbach's mother says Maria told a military investigator that she no longer believed Laurean was the father of her unborn child. However, Lauterbach's mother, Mary, says her daughter remained adamant that Laurean raped her. Laurean denied it. A few weeks before a scheduled rape hearing at Camp Lejeune, Lauterbach disappeared. Dewey Hudson, district attorney for Onslow County, said Laurean is scheduled for arraignment in early June, and is expected to enter a plea. "I cannot comment on any of the tests," Hudson said. He would not say how the DNA results might affect his case against Laurean. Through her attorney, Mary Lauterbach said the DNA test results don't answer bigger questions she has about whether the Marines did enough to protect her daughter or moved quickly enough to investigate her claims. "We do not believe that the result will have any effect on the continuing investigation or the trial," said Lauterbach's attorney Merle Wilberding.

(CNN) — The Marine accused of killing Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach, who was more than eight months pregnant, was not the father of her unborn child, a law enforcement source close to the murder investigation said Saturday.

Marine Cpl. Cesar Laurean, who is being held on a murder charge, is scheduled to be arraigned in June. The source, who reviewed a report completed earlier this month by the Defense Department’s Armed Forces Institute of Pathology, said Laurean’s DNA did not match that of the unborn child, who also died.

Laurean and Lauterbach were stationed at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. An autopsy showed that Lauterbach, 20, died from blunt-force trauma to the head. In January 2008, police unearthed her charred body from beneath a barbecue pit in Laurean’s backyard. She had disappeared the previous month.

Laurean was 22 when he was arrested in Mexico in April 2008. At the time, a Mexican reporter asked him whether he had killed Lauterbach. The Marine replied, “I loved her.”

Laurean has been indicted on charges including first-degree murder, financial card transaction fraud and obtaining property by false pretenses. North Carolina prosecutors allege that he killed Lauterbach on December 14 and used her ATM card 10 days later before fleeing to Mexico. He holds dual citizenship in the United States and Mexico.

The law enforcement source familiar with the case said a DNA swab was taken from Laurean by court order after he was extradited from Mexico in March to face charges in North Carolina. Mexican authorities agreed to the extradition in part because prosecutors took the death penalty off the table. Mexico does not have the death penalty.

Before her death, Lauterbach told the Marines that Laurean had raped her. The month before she disappeared, Lauterbach’s mother said Maria told a military investigator that she no longer believed Laurean was the father of her unborn child. However, her mother, Mary Lauterbach, said her daughter remained adamant that Laurean had raped her. Laurean denied the allegation.

A few weeks before a scheduled rape hearing at Camp Lejeune, Lauterbach disappeared.

Dewey Hudson, district attorney for Onslow County, said Laurean is scheduled to be arraigned in early June and is expected to enter a plea.

“I cannot comment on any of the tests,” Hudson said. He declined to say how the DNA results might affect the case against Laurean.

Through her attorney, Mary Lauterbach said the DNA test results do not answer her broader questions about whether the Marines did enough to protect her daughter or acted quickly enough to investigate her claims.

“We do not believe that the result will have any effect on the continuing investigation or the trial,” said Lauterbach’s attorney, Merle Wilberding.

**DNA: Marine suspect not father of slain Marine’s unborn child**

**JACKSONVILLE, North Carolina (CNN)** — DNA testing shows that Marine Cpl. Cesar Laurean was not the father of the unborn child carried by slain Marine Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach, authorities said.

Lauterbach, 20, was about eight months pregnant when she disappeared in December 2007 from Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. Her burned remains and those of her unborn child were later discovered in a fire pit behind Laurean’s home near Jacksonville.

Before her disappearance, Lauterbach had accused Laurean of rape. The DNA findings establish that Laurean did not father her child but do not, by themselves, resolve the sexual-assault allegation.

Investigators have said Lauterbach died from a blow to the head. Laurean became the focus of a nationwide manhunt after authorities alleged that he fled North Carolina shortly before the remains were found.

Laurean denied raping Lauterbach. Authorities said the homicide investigation would continue despite the paternity results.

counterfactuals.output:
# BREAKING: Former Marine Convicted of Killing Pregnant Colleague, Burying Her Beneath Backyard Fire Pit

**GOLDSBORO, N.C. — Aug. 23, 2010** — A North Carolina jury on Monday convicted former Marine Cpl. Cesar Armando Laurean of murdering a pregnant Marine who had accused him of rape, then burying her body beneath a fire pit in his backyard near Camp Lejeune.

After deliberating for roughly three hours, jurors found Laurean guilty of first-degree murder in the December 2007 death of 20-year-old Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach. He was also convicted of theft and fraud-related charges connected to his flight from authorities.

A judge sentenced Laurean to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Prosecutors could not seek the death penalty because Mexico agreed to extradite Laurean only after receiving assurances that he would not face execution.

## Remains found beneath backyard fire pit

Lauterbach, who was about eight months pregnant, disappeared from the Camp Lejeune area on Dec. 14, 2007. Her burned remains and those of her unborn son were discovered the following month in a shallow grave behind Laurean’s home near Jacksonville, North Carolina.

Investigators said Laurean attempted to conceal the burial site by constructing a concrete-block fire pit over it. Authorities searching the property found evidence of burning before uncovering the remains on Jan. 11, 2008.

An autopsy determined that Lauterbach died from blunt-force injuries to the head. Prosecutors said Laurean killed her with a metal object, burned her body and buried her in his yard.

## Victim had accused Laurean of sexual assault

Months before her death, Lauterbach reported that Laurean had raped her. Both Marines served in the same logistics unit at Camp Lejeune, one of the nation’s largest Marine Corps installations.

Laurean denied the sexual-assault accusation, and no trial had taken place before Lauterbach disappeared. Prosecutors argued that he killed her to prevent her from testifying and to protect himself from criminal prosecution and the destruction of his military career.

The case also raised questions about how the Marine Corps handles sexual-assault complaints, particularly when an accuser and the person accused serve in the same command.

Lauterbach’s family said she had been frightened and felt isolated during the months after reporting the alleged assault.

## Laurean fled to Mexico

By the time investigators focused on Laurean, he had left North Carolina. Authorities said he withdrew money, left behind misleading notes and traveled by bus into Mexico, where he had been born.

A nationwide and international manhunt followed. Mexican authorities arrested Laurean in April 2008 in the western state of Michoacán. He had reportedly been living under an assumed name and working odd jobs.

Mexico extradited him to the United States in April 2009 after American officials agreed not to pursue a death sentence.

## Defense disputed who carried out the killing

Laurean did not testify during the trial. His attorneys acknowledged that he helped dispose of Lauterbach’s body but argued that prosecutors had failed to prove he was the person who killed her.

The defense sought to cast suspicion on Laurean’s wife and challenged parts of the prosecution’s timeline. Jurors rejected that argument, accepting the state’s case that Laurean carried out the killing and took deliberate steps to hide the crime.

Prosecutors relied on forensic evidence, Laurean’s conduct after the disappearance, statements attributed to him and evidence recovered from his home and property.

## Family marks verdict after years-long case

The verdict brought a legal resolution nearly three years after Lauterbach vanished. Her relatives attended the proceedings and had pushed for accountability both in the criminal case and in the military’s handling of her assault complaint.

Lauterbach’s unborn child, whom she planned to name Gabriel, died with her.

The case drew national attention because of the brutality of the crime, Laurean’s flight across the border and the revelation that Lauterbach had reported sexual violence within the military before she was killed.

Laurean will serve the remainder of his life in prison without parole.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the law enforcement finding that Cesar Laurean’s DNA did not match Maria Lauterbach’s unborn baby, while explaining why prosecutors and the victim’s family say the result does not resolve the murder and rape allegations.
counterfactuals.output:
A DNA test found that former Marine Cpl. Cesar Laurean was not the biological father of Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach’s unborn child. Law-enforcement officials stressed, however, that the result was a paternity finding—not proof that Laurean had not sexually assaulted or killed her.

Lauterbach, who was about eight months pregnant when she disappeared from Camp Lejeune in December 2007, had accused Laurean of rape before her death. Prosecutors noted that a sexual assault does not necessarily result in pregnancy and that the child could have been conceived in a separate encounter. Thus, excluding Laurean as the father did not disprove her rape allegation.

Her family likewise said Maria had not based the rape accusation on a claim that Laurean fathered the baby. They argued that treating the paternity result as an exoneration would wrongly conflate two different questions: who fathered the child and whether Laurean assaulted her.

The DNA finding also did not address the murder evidence. Lauterbach’s burned remains and those of her fetus were found buried behind Laurean’s home near Jacksonville, North Carolina. Investigators said she died from blunt-force trauma, and Laurean fled to Mexico before being captured. Prosecutors maintained that the evidence surrounding her death—including the location and concealment of the body and Laurean’s flight—stood independently of the paternity issue. He was later convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison without parole.

Because Lauterbach was killed, the rape allegation could not be tested in the same way it might have been had she survived. The DNA result therefore excluded one possible biological link but did not resolve either the sexual-assault allegation or Laurean’s responsibility for her killing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**Paternity test adds new detail in Lauterbach murder case**

**JACKSONVILLE, N.C.** — Newly released DNA test results show that Cpl. Cesar Laurean was not the father of the unborn child carried by Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach, the pregnant Marine he is accused of killing.

The finding could become an issue in the prosecution of Laurean, although it does not resolve the central allegations against him. Authorities have said Lauterbach accused Laurean, a fellow Marine stationed at Camp Lejeune, of raping her and that the pending sexual-assault case may have provided a motive for her killing. The rape allegation was never adjudicated.

Lauterbach, 20, disappeared in December 2007 while about eight months pregnant. Her burned remains and those of her unborn child were found the following month in a fire pit in the backyard of Laurean’s home near Jacksonville. Investigators said she died from a blow to the head.

Laurean fled North Carolina before the remains were discovered and crossed into Mexico, according to authorities. After a three-month international search, Mexican police arrested him in April 2008 in the state of Michoacán. He was charged with first-degree murder and faced extradition proceedings.

Investigators initially examined whether Laurean could have been the father of Lauterbach’s child because of her sexual-assault accusation. The paternity results exclude him, but they do not establish whether an assault occurred or who killed Lauterbach.

The test could nevertheless be cited by the defense in challenging any suggestion that the pregnancy itself gave Laurean a reason to kill her. Prosecutors could argue that the more significant motive was the pending rape investigation and its possible consequences for Laurean’s military career.

Laurean is presumed innocent unless proved guilty.
